entities.summary:
Francisco Galcerán de Lloris y de Borja, known also as Francesco Borgia, was a significant, albeit unconsecrated, cardinal of the Catholic Church during the tumultuous late 15th and early 16th centuries. Born into the powerful Valencian Borgia family, his career epitomized the intricate fusion of aristocratic lineage, political ambition, and ecclesiastical authority characteristic of the Renaissance papacy. His rise, largely orchestrated by his uncle, Pope Alexander VI, highlights the pervasive nepotism and strategic use of church offices to consolidate familial power that defined the period, offering a vivid case study of the era's complex religious and political landscape.

Elevated to cardinal deacon in 1503, Lloris y de Borja held numerous influential benefices, including the bishoprics of Teano (1498–1500), Elne (1500–1505), and later the archdioceses of Reggio Calabria (1503) and Monreale (1505). While his cardinalate was posthumously ratified by Pope Pius III following Alexander VI's death, it solidified his status within the sacred college. He participated in the two papal conclaves of 1503, which successively elected Pius III and Julius II, primarily representing the residual Borgia faction's interests. His administrative acumen in managing these extensive ecclesiastical holdings contributed substantially to the Borgia family's immense wealth and political leverage across Italy and Spain.

entities.summary:
Francisco Galcerán de Lloris y de Borja, known also as Francisc de Lloris i de Borja in Catalan and Francesco Borgia in Italian, emerged as a prominent, albeit unconsecrated, cardinal within the Catholic Church during the tumultuous late 15th and early 16th centuries. Born in Valencia in 1470, his significance primarily stems from his close familial ties to the powerful Borgia dynasty, particularly his uncle, Pope Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia). This connection placed him directly within the intricate web of Renaissance papal politics, where nepotism, dynastic ambition, and ecclesiastical power struggles defined the era, making him a tangible representation of the Borgia's influence across the Iberian Peninsula and the Italian states.

Elevated to the cardinalate *in pectore* (in the breast) by Pope Alexander VI on 20 March 1493, Lloris y de Borja's cardinalate was not publicly declared until 1496, making him Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Sabina. His ecclesiastical career was marked by numerous appointments, including Bishop of Terni (1498), Bishop of Elne (1499), and Administrator of the Archdiocese of Monreale (1503-1505). He also served as Governor of Spoleto in 1498 and played a role in the papal curia, though his influence was more administrative and financial than theological or military, consistently working to consolidate the Borgia family's secular and spiritual authority through strategic placements of loyalists.
